 CORE

Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Compare and contrast the clinical, radiographic, and histologic characteristics of common
fibrous lesions of bone.
Discuss appropriate work up and diagnosis of fibrous lesions of bone.
Review general treatment principles for fibrous lesions of bone.
Nonossifying Fibroma
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Nonossifying fibroma (NOF) is a benign spindle cell tumor of bone containing osteoclast-like
giant cells. It generally is self-limiting.




NOTES
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
1/21

Epidemiology
Most lesions do not come to clinical attention.
Estimated to occur in as many as 30% to 40% of children
Most common tumor of bone
Peak incidence in individuals in their teenage years
Anatomy
Most arise in long bone metaphyses of the lower extremities.
Etiology
Unknown for sporadic cases
NOFs may occur in the presence of germline mutations, including NF1, Jaffe-Campanacci
syndrome, and KRAS.
Mutations in KRAS and FGFR1 have been identified in more than 80% of sporadic cases.
This finding suggests that NOFs are true neoplasms driven by activated mitogen-activated
protein kinase signaling.1
Natural History
Although lesions may grow along with the patient, at skeletal maturity the lesions ossify and
then appear sclerotic.
Malignant transformation has not been reported.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Typically asymptomatic and identified incidentally
Patients may have a pathologic fracture.
Imaging Studies
Radiographs demonstrate eccentric, metaphyseal, well-circumscribed lesions with a sclerotic
rim and lacking matrix.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
2/21

Can migrate to the diaphysis during years of bone growth
May have thin cortex and demonstrate mild expansion
Plain radiographs are diagnostic (Figure 1).
Figure 1 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the knee of an 8-year-old boy demonstrate
fibroxanthoma (arrows) identified as an incidental finding. Fibroxanthomas commonly are
diagnosed as an incidental finding. The fibroxanthoma is visualized much more clearly on the
lateral radiograph. (Reproduced from Parrish WM: Benign fibrous lesions and Langerhans cell
histiocytosis, in Biermann JS, Siegel GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal
Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 141-150.)
Pathology
Bland, spindle-shaped cells with a storiform growth pattern
Scattered osteoclast-type giant cells
Low mitotic activity
Diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
3/21

Most often, a NOF diagnosis is made based on plain radiographs. If the lesion has an atypical
appearance or if surgical management is considered, then tissue should be obtained for
diagnosis.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Most are managed via intermittent radiographic and clinical observation and without
procedural intervention.
Surgical Management
Rarely, curettage and bone grafting are considered for large and symptomatic lesions at risk of
pathologic fracture.
Pathologic fractures often are managed nonsurgically, followed by lesion observation or
curettage.
Internal fixation rarely is necessary.
After pathologic fracture, some lesions may accelerate in their healing.
Desmoplastic Fibroma of Bone
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Desmoplastic fibroma of bone is a locally aggressive bone tumor that is extremely rare. It
consists of bland spindle cells surrounded by collagen and has a histologic appearance similar
to that of desmoid-type fibromatosis.
Epidemiology
Exceptionally rare, accounting for less than 0.1% of all primary bone tumors
Mainly affects adolescents and young adults, with near equal sex distribution
Anatomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
4/21

Most frequently involves the mandible; however, more than 50% of reported cases are in the
femur, tibia, or pelvis.
Etiology
Unknown
Natural History
Desmoplastic fibroma does not have the ability to metastasize. It is slowly progressive and
locally aggressive.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients typically report at least several months of pain, with approximately 10% having a
pathologic fracture.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiolucent lesion with bony expansion and often intralesional trabeculation
May destroy cortical bone and extend into soft tissues, which distinguishes it from NOF
radiographically (Figure 2)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
5/21

Figure 2 Bilateral AP knee radiograph demonstrates desmoplastic fibroma. Radiographic
findings of desmoplastic fibroma are nonspecific but usually reveal a lucent lesion (arrow) with
some surrounding sclerosis. (Reproduced from Parrish WM: Benign fibrous lesions and
Langerhans cell histiocytosis, in Biermann JS, Siegel GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update:
Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2021, pp 141-150.)
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Characteristic low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted MRIs, in keeping with its fibrous
tissue and abundant collagen histology
Pathology
Grossly, it is firm, with a creamy-white color, and well defined.
Histopathology shows infiltrative growth with low cellularity, absent mitoses, and necrosis,
with bland spindle cells and a collagen matrix.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
6/21

Absence of GNAS mutation, absence of MDM2 amplification
Diagnosis
Diagnosis of desmoplastic fibroma of bone made via tissue diagnosis
Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis includes fibrous dysplasia; however, desmoplastic fibroma lacks
GNAS mutation. The absence of MDM2 amplification helps exclude a low-grade central
osteosarcoma.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Desmoplastic fibroma of bone is a separate entity from desmoid-type fibromatosis, and no
substantial evidence suggests that systemic agents that are active in the management of
desmoid-type fibromatosis are effective in the management of desmoplastic fibroma of bone.
Surgical Management
The rarity of this diagnosis limits knowledge of treatment strategies.

Management
Intralesional management, such as curettage, is associated with recurrence as high as
40%. En bloc resection and reconstruction should be considered because of the high
rates of local recurrence via intralesional procedures. Management depends on location
and the degree of involvement.
Fibrous Dysplasia
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
7/21

Overview

Overview
Fibrous dysplasia is a relatively common benign developmental anomaly of medullary
bone. It is characterized by bone marrow and cancellous bone replacement with
distorted, poorly organized mineralized bone and intervening fibrous tissue. It may be
monostotic, polyostotic, or associated with McCune-Albright syndrome or Mazabraud
syndrome. Although fibrous dysplasia may be identified incidentally, particularly if
polyostotic, it may result in osseous deformity and associated symptoms.
Epidemiology
Fibrous dysplasia is distributed equally by sex and affects all racial groups.
Monostotic disease accounts for approximately 70% of patients with fibrous dysplasia and
typically is diagnosed before age 30 years as an incidental finding.
Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia typically is diagnosed earlier in life, with patients reporting pain or
a pathologic fracture.
Etiology
Caused by postzygotic activating missense mutations of the GNAS gene on chromosome 20q13
This gene encodes the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein.
These proteins increase WNT/beta-catenin signaling, inhibiting maturation/differentiation of
osteoprogenitor cells.
Natural History
Malignant transformation rarely occurs.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
8/21

Monostotic fibrous dysplasia typically is an incidental finding. Patients with polyostotic variants
have pain or pathologic fracture.
The most common sites are the femur and craniofacial bones; however, every bone can be
affected. In the appendicular skeleton, lesions are most commonly metaphyseal or diaphyseal.
The classic location is the proximal femur in a skeletally maturing individual.
Fibrous dysplasia lesions also may be identified during workup for potential syndromes or
endocrine abnormalities.
Precocious puberty, which occurs in female patients more than male patients, is a symptom
of McCune-Albright syndrome. This often manifests as menstrual bleeding by age 2 years.
Oncogenic osteomalacia may occur, related to renal phosphate wasting caused by increased
levels of fibroblast growth factor-23.
Physical Examination
Café-au-lait spots with irregular, coast of Maine contours occur in 50% of patients with
polyostotic disease. These areas are most commonly located on the neck, lower lumbar spine,
face, and lips.
Mazabraud syndrome, which is rare, is the association of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia with
multiple soft-tissue myxomas. The myxomas often are found overlying the involved bones and
close to joints, typically in the lower extremities.
Imaging Studies
Most diagnoses can be made based on plain radiographs (Figure 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
9/21

Figure 3 Bilateral AP lower leg radiograph demonstrates polyostotic fibrous dysplasia in the
tibiae and fibulae (arrows). Weakening of the bone may lead to bowing of the tibia or a varus
deformity in the femoral neck, referred to as a shepherd crook deformity. (Reproduced from
Parrish WM: Benign fibrous lesions and Langerhans cell histiocytosis, in Biermann JS, Siegel GW,
eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 141-150.)
Radiography
Lesions will be well circumscribed and without aggressive features in the medullary space of
the diaphysis/metaphysis.
The lesion has a characteristic ground-glass matrix. The bony trabeculae appear as if
smudged. This appearance is a result of woven bone and fibrous tissue replacing the normal
trabecular pattern.
One of the small number of potentially polyostotic bone lesions
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
10/21

Long-standing lesions may be associated with remodeling, such as in the shepherd crook
deformity of an affected proximal femur in varus. This deformity is the result of multiple
microfractures because of bone weakness.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
The typical appearance is decreased signal intensity on T1-weighted MRIs, increased signal
intensity on T2-weighted MRIs, and contrast avid. This appearance represents a cellular tissue
with high water content. Areas of cystic degeneration may be present, often confounding the
diagnosis with that of a unicameral bone cyst.
Bone Scintigraphy
May show mild to moderate uptake; however, bone scintigraphy typically is not performed
except if polyostotic disease is a concern.
Pathology
The gross tissue appearance is firm tan or gray, with a gritty texture from bony spicules. Cysts
may be present.
Histology reveals fibrous and osseous components, with uncommon mitoses. The fibrous
portion shows bland fibroblastic cells admixed with an osseous component of irregular
curvilinear woven bone. Osteoblasts are inconspicuous. A key finding is a lack of osteoblastic
rimming around bony spicules.
At low-power magnification, this entity has been described as having an alphabet soup
appearance.
Diagnosis
If a lesion is identified incidentally on imaging studies and fibrous dysplasia is suspected,
management may consist of observation in the absence of symptoms. Otherwise, a tissue
diagnosis is made at the time of surgical management or via image-guided biopsy.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
11/21

The management of fibrous dysplasia generally is nonsurgical. The goal of management is to
prevent deformity and pain.
Diphosphonates and denosumab are options to decrease fracture rates and pain, particularly
in patients with polyostotic disease.
Surgical Management
Surgical treatment may be considered in patients with ongoing pain, deformity, or nonunion
and for stabilization of femur fractures.
Bone grafting typically is unsuccessful because the new ingrowth of bone is affected by the
same process. If grafting is performed, cortical struts should be used rather than nonstructural
grafts.
The surgical goal is structural and functional restoration rather than removal of the disease.
Intramedullary devices are favored over plates.
Although embolization typically is not performed, bleeding may be considerable in patients
with large areas of disease.
Osteofibrous Dysplasia
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
A benign fibro-osseous tumor in long bones, osteofibrous dysplasia (OFD) typically occurs in
the anterior cortex of the tibia during childhood.
Epidemiology
Rare, accounting for less than 0.5% of all primary bone tumors
OFD is unlikely after age 15 years.
Anatomy
Typically arising in the proximal to middle third of the tibia
Ipsilateral involvement of fibula observed in 20% of patients
Involvement in long bones besides the tibia or fibula is extremely rare.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
12/21

Etiology
Unknown; rare familial cases reported.
Causative genetic aberrations are unidentified; however, GNAS mutations are absent.
Trisomies 7, 8, 12, and 22 have been reported.
Natural History
The existence of a continuum from OFD to adamantinoma is controversial; most surgeons
suggest that a continuum does not exist; however, rarely, adamantinoma has been reported
to arise from a preexisting OFD.
Osteofibrous dysplasia-like adamantinoma disease more closely mimics OFD.
Lesions may regress spontaneously or stabilize at skeletal maturity but require observation to
avoid substantial deformity.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients usually have painless swelling over the anterior leg.
Imaging Studies
Particularly consider radiographs for a lesion of the anterior tibial shaft diaphyseal cortex
Radiographs demonstrate an eccentric, well-circumscribed cortical lesion with areas of
sclerosis and areas without matrix.
The cortex may demonstrate thinning or expansion.
Does not usually involve the periosteum, which would suggest adamantinoma
May have bowing or pseudarthrosis
On imaging alone, may be identical to adamantinoma (Figure 4)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
13/21

Figure 4 AP radiograph of a lower leg demonstrates osteofibrous dysplasia (arrow),
occasionally referred to as Campanacci disease. The bubbly appearance involving the midtibia
is a classic radiographic finding. (Reproduced from Parrish WM: Benign fibrous lesions and
Langerhans cell histiocytosis, in Biermann JS, Siegel GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update:
Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2021, pp 141-150.)
Pathology
Grossly, the appearance is solid, white/yellow, and gritty.
Confined to the cortex
Histology
Woven bone with prominent osteoblastic rimming, surrounded by bland fibrous tissue
Mitoses are rare.
Diagnosis
Made based on imaging features and tissue biopsy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
14/21

Differential Diagnosis
OFD is distinguished from fibrous dysplasia based on imaging studies. In terms of pathology,
OFD has osteoblastic rimming, and GNAS gene mutations are absent.
Differential diagnosis includes adamantinoma, which also typically involves the tibia. Dissimilar
from patients with OFD, patients with adamantinoma have a median age of 25 to 35 years at
the time of presentation. In terms of histology, adamantinoma has epithelial cell clusters.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Surgical management should be avoided, if possible, with bracing used if necessary. Close
observation is recommended.
Surgical Management
Considered in patients with deformity or pseudoarthrosis, impending or pathologic fracture,
or severe symptoms
Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is a neoplastic clonal proliferation of myeloid dendritic cells
with a macrophage (histiocytic) phenotype.
LCH may be unifocal or multifocal within the bone or it may have multisystem involvement.
A misguided myeloid differentiation model of pathogenesis has been proposed.
Activating mitogen-activated protein kinase mutations at pluripotent hematopoietic, tissue-
restricted, or local levels result in multisystem, multifocal, or unifocal LCH, respectively.
Epidemiology
The annual incidence in children is approximately 5 cases per 1 million individuals; in adults,
the incidence is between 1 to 2 cases per 1 million individuals.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
15/21

A mild male predominance exists. LCH is more common among individuals of European and
Hispanic descent.
Anatomy
Bone involvement predominately involves the skull, femur, vertebrae, pelvis, ribs, and
mandible.
Multisystem LCH has preferential involvement of the skin, liver, and spleen in addition to bone.
In the appendicular skeleton, lesions typically are in the diaphysis.
Etiology
Unknown
Natural History
Unifocal disease only rarely affects mortality. Multisystem LCH is associated with less than 20%
mortality, with prolonged therapy.
Progression from focal to multisystem LCH may occur and typically is observed in infants.
Classification
Single-system LCH is defined by involvement of one organ or system and is further classified
as unifocal or multifocal.
Multisystem LCH is defined by involvement of two or more organs or systems.
The World Health Organization does not recommend referring to a solitary lesion as
eosinophilic granuloma or histiocytosis X.
Referring to multiple lesions as Hand-Schüller-Christian disease or referring to disseminated
LCH as Letterer-Siwe disease also is not recommended.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Single-system LCH of bone usually is observed in older children or adults in the form of a
painful bone lesion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
16/21

Multisystem LCH is observed in younger children and infants; in addition to painful bone
lesions, patients may have fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and/or skin lesions.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
In the frequently involved flat bones, such as the skull, a punched-out lesion is typical (Figure
5).
Figure 5 AP (A) and lateral (B) skull radiographs demonstrate a punched-out lesion (arrow) in
the skull. This is a typical appearance of an eosinophilic granuloma lesion in the skull.
(Reproduced from Parrish WM: Benign fibrous lesions and Langerhans cell histiocytosis, in
Biermann JS, Siegel GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 141-150.)
Vertebra plana is a classic finding in patients who have spinal LCH with vertebral body
involvement alone (Figure 6).
Figure 6 Images show eosinophilic granuloma. A, Lateral radiograph of a spine demonstrates
eosinophilic granuloma (arrow). Eosinophilic granuloma may result in vertebra plana if the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
17/21

spine is affected. Vertebra plana occurs of collapse of the anterior cortex of the vertebral body
occurs. B, Sagittal T1-weighted MRI of a spine shows vertebra plana (arrow). A low signal
intensity is observed in the vertebral body. Disk spaces above and below the affected levels
are preserved. C, Sagittal T2-weighted MRI of the spine of a patient with Langerhans cell
histiocytosis shows vertebra plana (arrow) with a high signal intensity. D, Sagittal, T1-weighted
contrast-enhanced MRI of a spine shows diffuse enhancement of a lesion (arrow). (Reproduced
from Parrish WM: Benign fibrous lesions and Langerhans cell histiocytosis, in Biermann JS,
Siegel GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 141-150.)
In the appendicular skeleton, a radiolucent lesion in the diaphysis is common and may have
periosteal reaction (Figure 7).
Figure 7 AP radiograph of the femur of an 8-year-old patient with eosinophilic granuloma
demonstrates an onion-skin appearance indicating periosteal reaction (arrow). The differential
diagnosis should include Ewing sarcoma or osteomyelitis. (Reproduced from Parrish WM:
Benign fibrous lesions and Langerhans cell histiocytosis, in Biermann JS, Siegel GW, eds:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy
of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 141-150.)
In terms of radiographic appearance, the differential diagnosis often includes a primary bone
malignancy and osteomyelitis. Therefore, LCH has been called a great mimicker.
Bone Scintigraphy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fibrous/Histiocytic Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004044
18/21

Because technetium-99m bone scintigraphy demonstrates only 35% of lesions, a skeletal
survey is more reliable for identifying multifocal osseous disease.
Pathology

Pathology
In terms of histopathology, LCH cells are oval, with irregular nuclear contours and pale
eosinophilic cytoplasm. On low-power magnification, LCH shows high cellularity, with a
characteristic milieu, including eosinophils and osteoclast-like giant cells. Electron
microscopy reveals cytoplasmic Birbeck granules, which have a tennis-racket shape with
a zipperlike appearance. Immunohistochemically, LCH cells express CD1a (related to
MHC proteins), CD207 (langerin), and S100, among others. Gene mutations involving the
mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway are recorded in more than 85% of patients.
Diagnosis
Made via tissue diagnosis
Differential Diagnosis
Before a tissue diagnosis is made, the clinical and radiographic features have a wide range of
differential diagnoses, including osteomyelitis and Ewing sarcoma.
Management
Solitary bone lesions often are self-limiting or heal reliably after biopsy or curettage. The use of
steroid injections also has been reported.
Patients with multifocal and multisystem LCH should be referred to specialists in (typically
pediatric) medical oncology. Systemic treatment options include methotrexate, vinblastine,
and corticosteroids.
Spine lesions rarely require surgical management.
Mark as Complete
